Note: Fifty of everything: fifty relics worn, fifty runes in the sack, fifty cards in the hand. It is the stress test for the three rows that share one widget - the hand, the worn relics and the sack are the same draggable, overlapping row at three widths - and it is kept rather than deleted because how they behave when full is a question worth looking at again. Each row packs inside its own pane, so none of them can squeeze another; resting the cursor on any of them raises the card under it whole, on the same tick its tooltip appears; and any of the three can be dragged into a different order. Fifty relics is possible at all because there is no ceiling on how many a duelist may wear - combat.MaxWornRelics was deleted on 2026-09-17 and what a run wears is combat.DefaultRelicSlots or whatever the run is carrying, which this sets to fifty. Nothing here is tuned: fifty relics firing into one sum is a picture of a layout rather than a balance question.

A run already under way, which is the state nothing else here boots into. Every other fixture is a question about one mechanic on an otherwise empty run; this one asks what the screen looks like when the player has been climbing for a while - five fingers full, runes in the sack, stones in the pouch, a purse worth spending and a duelist carrying a wound. Floor 3, middle room. The relics are picked to be told apart rather than to combo: one of each rarity so the pane shows all three borders, and five different families so no two cards are the same picture. Nothing here is tuned for a win - it is a fixture for looking at a laid-out screen, and the deck, the enemy and the draw are all the game's own. The seed is pinned rather than the deck replaced, so the hand is whatever the real shuffle deals and is the same hand every launch.

The Card Full House, dealt on purpose: three Cuts and two Braces out of a hand of eight, which is 5 AP and pays 3.42x. It is the hand that says most about how the ladder is counted, because both halves of it are things a player has to be told. The rung matches on CONCEPT - data/hands.json writes match concept, groups [3, 2] - so the three Cuts are a set because they are Cuts, and the colors they happen to wear are worth nothing to it; recolor every card in this hand and the multiplier does not move. And the two Braces are DEFEND cards that join the hand like anything else: they carry a form and an element, they count toward the rung, and they bring no damage with them - so the hits are three 0.5x slashes each under a 3.42x multiplier, and the shields go up beside the hits rather than instead of them. The other three cards - a Flinch, a Jab and a Block - are there to be left behind, so the hand is a choice rather than the only five cards in the row. Giant Bat, 15 AP and a dummy, and it shares the shields fixture's deck so the refill behaves the same way. See ASCEND_DUEL_SCENARIO=shields for the defences on their own.

The shields, on their own: what a defend card raises, what one eats, and how the break is drawn. No relics at all, so nothing on the screen is multiplying or recoloring anything and the only thing moving is the defence. The deck is two thirds defend cards across all five colors - Flinch at 0 AP, Brace at 1, Block at 2, Guard at 3 - with a thin seam of attacks so a turn can still form a hand and the shields can be watched going up beside the hits rather than instead of them. 15 AP, so a turn is a choice of which five cards rather than which five are affordable; remember combat.MaxActions still caps the turn at five cards however cheap they are, and one card raises at most five shields while a duelist holds as many as the turn paid for. The opponent is a Giant Bat because its deck has three clearly different blows - Nip at 50, Swoop at 100 and Drain at 200 - which is what makes the rule visible: a shield eats the creature's HEAVIEST blow, not its first, and it decides that at the top of the creature's turn. Watch the beat between the two turns, where the blocked pips fly out of the duelist card into the card they kill and the crack opens across its face. The pip row along the bottom of the duelist card draws at most six - screens.maxShieldPips - so a turn that raises ten draws a full row and the true count is on the engine. Against a dummy, so it can be watched as many times as it takes rather than survived.

The deal, the flip cascade and the sort, which is how every hand in a fight now arrives - see screens/combat_deal.go. Frozen Lightning, Glacier and Permafrost are worn in that order, so the cascade CHAINS and then doubles back: lightning goes to ice under ring one, ice goes to earth under ring two, and earth comes back to ice under ring three. Every lightning, ice and earth card in the deck therefore lands on ice, and a card can be watched going ice, earth, ice across three beats - which is the thing three rings are here to show, because a run wearing the middle relic alone would end on earth. The fire cards are the bystanders: no ring names them, so they sit still through all three beats and the row has something to be compared against. What to watch is the order - cards fly out of the pile left to right in the order the shuffle gave them, then each ring in turn rattles, rocks and lights while every card it touches rattles and morphs at once, and only then does the row sort itself. Press E for the element sort, which is where sorting LAST earns itself: under the default cost sort the element is only a tiebreak and the row barely moves, where on E it reorganises around what the cascade just did. Play a turn and the refill runs the whole sequence again over the cards it deals. Against a dummy, 15 AP, so it can be watched as many times as it takes rather than survived.

The five dual-status rings drawn on 2026-09-12 that carry a fire, ice or lightning rule, worn at once so the artwork can be read on the pane at the size a player actually sees it - Scald, Wildfire, Hoarfrost, Brittle and Palsy. It is a batch of art rather than an interaction, which is what RelicSlots exists for: the shipped cap is five, so looking at nine new rings used to mean buying one, selling it and buying the next. The art is the question, but the rules are worth watching too, because every one of these applies TWO statuses off one attack: the hand is a fire slash, an ice slash, a lightning crush and two more of the same colors, so a single turn puts BURNED, CHILLED, SHOCKED and WEAKENED on the badge row under the creature's fraction at once. Against a dummy, so the statuses can be stacked and read rather than killed off; 15 AP so the choice is which cards rather than which are affordable.

The other seven relics drawn on 2026-09-12: the four dual-status rings on earth and arcane - Caldera, Tremor, Blightfire and Millstone - plus the three records whose art is not a ring at all. The Sundering is an obsidian scimitar and The Bruise an obsidian mace, and they are the reason this fixture exists as well as the art: a relic is the category and a ring is one kind of it, so this is the page where a weapon and a ring are worn in the same row and can be told apart at a glance. The Jar of Metal is the third, and it is the one that says nothing until cards are LEFT in hand - it reads crush cards kept, so playing three of these five is a different turn from playing all five. The hand is earth and arcane in slash and crush, so Sundering fires on the slashes, Bruise on the crushes, and all four rings on the colors. RelicSlots is 7, which is under combat.MaxWornRelics and over the shipped cap. Against a dummy, 15 AP.

A fight that cannot end, on the real starting deck against whichever creature the climb dealt. Both duelists carry 999999 life and the clock is lifted to 999 rounds, so every blow, every shield break, every status and every signal can be played with for as long as it is interesting - the thing that is otherwise five rounds and a death away. The creature is a real record with a real portrait and a real deck, so it still swings back and the exchange still reads the way it reads in a run; what is gone is the ending. Add Relics, Deck or Runes to this entry and it becomes a bench for whatever is being looked at. Note both health bars sit at a fraction nothing will visibly move, which is the mechanic rather than a broken bar.

A deck of nothing but slashes, against a dummy that cannot die, so a form-axis hand can be built over and over without a fight ending. Written by go run ./tools/scenariodeck -form slash -size 40 and pasted in literally, which is the whole argument for a generator over a filter vocabulary: what is in the file is the list, so it can be read and checked. Every rung of the form ladder up to Five of a Kind is reachable every turn here, which is the deal a real deck almost never gives you - so it is the bench for a form-hand relic, a stone on a form rung, or just watching what a Form Full House looks like when it lands. Swap the -form for stab or crush, or take the dummy off, and it is a different bench.

A deck the wildcard rune has already been spent on, so the first thing on screen is an altered card rather than a shop three fights away. Half the deck is wild - a fire Jab, an ice Cut and an arcane Brace - and the other half is ordinary, in four colors that agree with nothing. Watch two things: the wash over the whole card, which is where an upgrade is said as of 2026-09-09, and the hand line, which names an elemental rung off a set of cards that share no color at all. Note the form mark stays hueless on a wild card and keeps its element on every other upgrade. A Motley is in the sack too, for spending on a card that is not wild yet.

The two gambling upgrades, already on cards, so the roll can be watched rather than bought toward. Four gold Jabs and four silver Cuts, with an ordinary Bash and Thump beside them for comparison; the opening hand holds one of each. Play the metals every turn and read the feed: gold announces +1 DMG or +5 max life on roughly two turns in five and the fighter card's stats move as it does, silver drops 10 into the purse on one in five. What to check is that a grant survives the round - the bonus lands on the run, so the next fight opens with it - and that a losing roll says nothing rather than saying nothing happened. A Golden and a Silver are in the sack for putting one metal over the other, which is what last-one-wins looks like.

A silver card and a chromatic one in the same hand, which neither the metals nor the wildcards entry can give you: the question is how the two upgrades read against each other on one table. The silver Cut writes nothing about its metal on the face at all - the sheen is what names it - where the wild Jab carries the five-band wash, keeps its form mark hueless, and says ANY ELEMENT. Both explain themselves in the tooltip and both are titled in their own ink: CHROMATIC letter by letter across the five bands, SILVER in one lifted gray over the odds it gambles at. Hover both, and check the silver card is identifiable without the hover. A gold Thrust and two plain cards are beside them so a sheen has something to be a sheen against. A Motley and a Silver are in the sack for putting either upgrade onto a card that has neither.

Every upgrade except the two metals, one to a card, filling the opening hand: heal, shield, damage-on-play, scale-in-combo, damage-in-hand, scale-in-hand, vitae-in-hand and the wildcard, in that order left to right. It exists to answer one question - are ten upgrades ten cards a player can tell apart at a glance, in a row, on the table rather than on a sheet. Eight of the colors are placeholders standing on a wheel that has no room left, so what to look for is the pairs that collide: the heal's rose against the relic pink, and the three cool held ones against each other. Note the wildcard is the only card whose form mark goes hueless. Run the metals scenario for gold and silver.

Bob, from the top, on the real starting deck. The seed and the opening creature are not here: they are in data/tutorial.json, because the lesson's promises - four cards of one color, one of them a shield, a turn that wounds without killing so the creature swings back - are facts about that deal against that creature, and a second copy of them here is a second copy to drift. This entry now says only 'teach it whatever the profile thinks', which is the one thing the real trigger cannot do and the only way to see the tutorial twice.

The reward screen wearing the Cloud Necklace: an essence takes two cards rather than one. Select two cards in the row, then click an essence, and watch both change together. Sell the necklace in the shop to see the row go back to asking for one.
The reward screen with something to say: a purse big enough to earn interest, a fight won on 63 life, and the stairway's award. Watch the three sentences type and each figure fly to the duelist card.

The shop with money to spend, two fingers already full, a rune in the sack and a wound to heal. Straight to the shelf without playing three duels to reach it, and hurt enough that a Salve is worth buying.
A stairway protector on his own card: name, title, portrait and a deck out of bosses.json rather than the roster. The first stairway a run reaches is fight 2, which is where this opens.

Does an echoed fire card grow Enflamed three times? Play the Skewer first: it leads the turn, so Echo lands it three times - three hits, three lines under it - and Enflamed should step 0.3x rather than 0.1x.

The most hits the hand dialog can be asked to draw: five cards, the lead one echoed twice, so seven lines of arithmetic at once - three stacked under the lead card and one under each of the others. The type is never shrunk, so watch how the lines overlap and where they run off the screen.

Atrophy deals the 3 AP attacks as 2 AP ones, so the whole hand fits a turn â€” and the Block at the end of it is what resets Momentum, so the growth should climb 0.2x a round and then drop to nothing.

Two flips and a demotion, so the deck panel's ALTERATIONS toggle has something to show. Open the draw pile: earth and lightning are dealt as fire, the 3 AP attacks are dealt a rung down, and AS OWNED puts all of it back. FULL/PLAYED after a round or two.

The board piece: a sack holding one of each shape a rune can take, clicked in the consumables pane on the top row - select the cards in the hand first, then click the rune. It is here because a rune is otherwise two screens away - bought from the shop shelf, then spent between the turns of the fight after it - so seeing the dialog at all meant playing to a shop and winning a room. Siphon is the rider (a card that heals you as it is played, for the rest of the run), Unmake eats two cards, Mimic copies one and the copy joins the hand you are holding, Graft makes the first card you click into the second, and Hoard needs no target at all and so fires with nothing selected.

The four riders that pay for a card you do NOT play, plus the two that pay for one you do. Attach Patience or Spite or Tithe to a card, then leave that card in the hand and press DUEL! - every hit gets bigger, or the fight log says 'kept back for 3 vitae', on every turn you go on holding it. Hunger is the opposite question: it only pays if its card is one of the cards the hand was formed from, which a turn can play a card without doing. Aegis puts a Jab in the shield business. It is here because none of this is on a card face yet - the tooltip prose is the only readout, so the way to check the arithmetic is to hold the card and watch the hits.

The eight recoloring and reforming runes, two cards each. The five marks paint a pair of cards an element; the three staves change what a pair COUNTS AS on the form axis without changing the cards - so point Maulstave at two Braces and you have two cards that still shield and now make a crush pair. That is a legal weird thing on the owner's call, not a hole in the checking. Watch the corner mark and the cost ticks for the recolor; watch the hands panel for the reform.

Three rock showers in the sack. Each one needs no target, so it is taken on the click, and the panel stays up showing the three stones it just handed over - they go into the run's POUCH, not onto the ladder. Win the fight and the shop's S button is where they are spent: Use puts one on its rung, Sell pays 5. For the shop half on its own without the fight, see stones-in-the-pouch.

Opens on the shop carrying five stones, which is the other half of the rock shower. The S button in the corner beside D and C is the pouch; click a stone to arm it and two tabs hang under it - green Use puts it on its rung for the rest of the run, crimson Sell pays 5 vitae. The hands panel next door is where to check a Use actually moved the rung. It is here because a carried stone is otherwise a rune bought, a fight won and a shower spent away.

Four cheap attacks across three forms and four elements, plus a defense: one turn that earns Spectrum, Weaponmaster and Arsenal at once, which is three toasts in a row and the only way to see the queue drain. Poke, Nick and Tap are 1 AP, so the whole thing fits the 6 AP turn. Elementalist is deliberately not reachable from this hand - five elements needs five attacks, and a turn holds five cards, so it and Arsenal cannot both land on one turn. The awards are written to the real profile; point ASCEND_DUEL_PROFILE at an empty directory to see them land again.

A Luck and a Chimera in the sack, which is the whole of it since the sack holds two. Luck needs no target: click it and it rolls once - 1 in 5 for +1 DMG, 1 in 5 for +5 max life, 3 in 5 for nothing. Watch the duelist card's DMG and life bar, because a dud looks exactly like a click that did nothing and that is the mechanic rather than a bug. Then read the Chimera's face: it stops saying REPEAT LAST RUNE and starts saying COPIES LUCK, and clicking it rolls again. Spend the Chimera FIRST to see the other half - with nothing spent yet it has nothing to copy and is drawn dim.

Every kind of card signal in one hand, so the fireworks can be looked at rather than played toward. The metals are at 5, the shipping odds - a gold Jab pays on two plays in five and a silver Cut on one in five, so several turns may be wanted; the heal Thrust and the two vitae-in-hand Slices fire on every single play, which is what makes the hand worth queueing even on a turn the metals miss. Certainty is not available and that is the design: combat.LuckOutcomes refuses a die with no losing face, because a gamble that always pays is a purchase. Queue the gold Jab, the silver Cut and the heal Thrust together and press DUEL!. The order is the thing to check: the two Slices left in the hand throw their crimson vitae first, together, and the hits do not begin until their figures have landed on the duelist card - then each played card bursts on the beat its own figure sets off into its hit, and every signal holds the hits where they are. The burst and the figure leave together, in one color per card: gold for the gold Jab, silver for the silver Cut, the rose for the heal, crimson for the cards kept back. And a losing roll says nothing at all, which is the mechanic rather than a missing picture.

An easy button: five Pulverizes in one element, a budget that pays for all of them, and the weakest creature in the game. Press DUEL! once and the fight is over, so the reward screen's essence offer is one click away.

What a growing relic's counter looks like as it grows. The Heart is worn alone - +5 HP now and 5 more for every fight won - so the disc in the corner of its card is the only figure on the pane that moves, and it starts at 5 rather than at nothing, which is the thing the badge is easiest to misread about. The deck is forty Pulverizes in one element and the budget pays for five of them, so a fight is one press of DUEL! and the counter can be watched across four or five wins in a couple of minutes: 5, 10, 15. Read it in three places - the relic pane during the fight, the shop's worn row between them, and the tooltip, which is where the figure is said in words. The Giant Bat is the opening room's own creature and the climb takes over from the second fight, so the opponents get real without the deck doing.

The counter badge on all three rarity borders at once, and Momentum's is the one the fixture is named for. Momentum is common, so its disc is the bone border and its figure is drawn in black; Enflamed is uncommon and its green disc takes the card's own surface; the Shieldbearer is rare and its gold disc takes black again - the ink is picked off how light the disc actually is rather than off the rarity, so these three are the whole of what there is to check. All three grow, so all three carry a figure from the first frame: 1.0, 1.0, 1.0. Momentum steps 0.2x on every turn that raises no shields and resets the moment a defend card is played, the Shieldbearer steps 0.2x for each shield card played, and Enflamed steps 0.1x every time a fire attack lands - so one Brace moves two of them in opposite directions and is the quickest way to see a figure change. It is a dummy fight on the real starting deck with a 15 AP budget, because what is being looked at is a badge rather than a duel: play turns for as long as the figures are interesting. See ASCEND_DUEL_SCENARIO=the-heart for the flat counter, which is the other shape the badge takes.

Twenty-five cards in the hand at once, which is three times what a fight ever deals and is here to answer one question: what does the row look like when handPitch runs out of room. There is no floor on the pitch - see combat_actionbox.go, where the deliberate choice is that a hand which has to be scrolled or truncated is worse than one which has to be hovered - so the row lands exactly on the band's width whatever is in it and the cards overlap until they are stripes of color. That is what makes the five elements the thing to look at: the border and the left column are what survive compression, and the effect text and the form mark are the first things to go. Five cards in each color and all four forms across them, with costs from 0 to 3, so the tick column varies down the row as well as across it. Note the hand refills to eight the moment a turn is played - handTarget reads handSize and nothing here widens it - so the twenty-five is the opening hand and one DUEL! ends it. Against a dummy at 15 AP so the row can be hovered, dragged and re-sorted for as long as it is interesting; press E and C to see the compressed row reorganise.

The shop with a large vial of essence standing on the goods row, which is the only place in the game an essence is bought rather than given. The seed is pinned so the row is the same every launch: shop-shelf rolls its two goods off a fresh run code and stocks rocks and runes often enough that looking at the vial meant relaunching until one turned up. Buy the vial, pick a card in the lower row, then click a lit essence.

Every attack the turn paid for lands its own hit, whether or not it made the rung. The hand is two ice shields and five attacks in four colours, so the two cases are one click apart. Take the two shields and one attack: they form the Pair on themselves and throw no hit, the attack is in no rung, and it lands its hit anyway at the Pair's multiplier. Take the two earth Jabs and add the fire Bash: the Card Pair is the two Jabs, the Bash's hit rides at its rate and burns as well. The budget is wide and nothing dies, so every combination can be tried against the same bat.

A full top row: four rings worn and four runes in the sack, which is the row every between-turns gesture is made from and is otherwise two shops and a won fight away. Two of the rings are flips into fire, so the deal cascade plays two beats over every hand and each ring toasts as its own colours change; the third multiplies fire and the fourth multiplies a Pair, so both toast into the hits when the hand pays. The four runes are one of each shape a hand's morph can take - Embermark recolours two cards where they stand, Mimic copies one, Unmake eats two, and Hunger writes an upgrade onto one - so select the cards first and click the rune second, and watch the row change under the cursor. The sack holds four against a capacity of two on purpose: an over-full sack reads as the 4/2 it is and the pane tightens to draw all four, which is the thing a fixture can show and a bought sack cannot. It is a dummy at 12 AP, so any hand is payable and nothing here ends.

Twenty-five in the hand, twenty-five on the fingers and four in the sack, so all three overlapping rows are on screen at once and at three different pitches. It is the fixture for one question: when cards overlap, does the card the cursor raises match the card the tooltip describes. ui.RaisedSeat counts from the top of the stack down, because the last seat drawn is the one actually on top - so the raise is right by construction wherever it is used, and any row whose hover walks the other way will raise one card and explain the card behind it. Rest the cursor on a sliver in each row and read the panel against the card that comes up whole. The relic row and the hand are at the same pitch as each other and the sack is far tighter, four cards into two seats, which is where the disagreement is widest. A dummy at 15 AP, so the hand can be hovered, dragged and re-sorted for as long as it is interesting; the three sort tabs reorder the row under the cursor, which is the other half of the same question.

Fourteen runes against a sack that holds two, and twenty rings on ten fingers. It is the row-packing fixture between the four-rune bench and the fifty-of-everything one: the sack is seven times over-full and reads as the 14/2 it is, so its cards are slivers of each other, while the relic pane packs twenty at a pitch the row was never sized for. Both draw front to back, so the card under the cursor is the last one covering it - rest on any sliver and the card that comes up whole is the card the panel describes and the card a press takes. All twenty rings are elemental flips and they chain, so a hand arriving plays a beat per ring that actually changes something and the ones that touch nothing stay still. The fourteen runes are every shape one can take: five recolours, four form changes, a destroy, a copy, a graft, a play upgrade and the wildcard. A dummy at 12 AP, so nothing ends.

Ten runes, one for every shape a rune can take, in a sack that can be read rather than spent. All nine targets the rules have are here - Ashmark recolors two cards, Maulstave reforms two, Graft makes one card into another, Mimic copies one, Unmake eats two, Gildstone and the wildcard seal each write an upgrade onto one, Chimera repeats whatever was spent last, Rockfall fills the pouch and Hoard pays straight into the purse - so every branch of runeTipLines is on one row and can be compared side by side. That is the question it answers: which of Rider, Value and Count a rune's panel reads depends entirely on its target, which is what makes a rune the least readable record in data/ and its tooltip the only place the answer is spelled out. Two of the ten stress the panel hardest - the wildcard seal and Gildstone each carry an authored line break and a word the coloring has to claim. Against a dummy so nothing ends while the row is being read, and 15 AP so the hand is a choice rather than a budget.

Ten rings on the fingers and ten runes in the sack, on a fight that can be won in one press. It is the fixture for what the worn row and the sack look like when both are full of things that do not match each other: ten different families, so no two rings are the same picture, and all three rarity borders on screen at once. The ten runes are one for every shape a rune can take, which is the set ASCEND_DUEL_SCENARIO=ten-runes reads on its own. The hand is five Pulverizes in one element against the weakest creature in the game with a budget that pays for all of them, so DUEL! ends the fight and the reward screen and then the shop are each one click away - and the purse is set well past the dearest thing on a shelf, so the shop is a row to be looked at rather than a sum to be counted. Nothing here is tuned: ten relics firing into one sum is a picture of a laid-out screen rather than a balance question.

Two flips that chain and the two life relics, on a real duelist with a readable health bar. The deck is half lightning and half ice; Frozen Lightning is worn left of Meltdown, so a lightning card is dealt ice and then fire - two steps, two beats, a toast on each ring - while a native ice card takes the second step alone. That is combat.FlipSteps carrying a running element through the worn list, and the worn order is what decides it: swap the two rings and lightning stays lightning, because Meltdown reads the card before Frozen Lightning has touched it. Vampiric Fang gives back 3/10 of every hit and The Tear restores 1/4 of maximum life at the top of each turn, so the two life gestures are side by side: a drain leaves the body it was taken out of, a regeneration leaves the ring that made it. It has NO Hand on purpose - a plugged hand is seated straight out of the run and never goes through drawHand, so it would show the cards unflipped and the cascade would not run at all. It is not a dummy for the same kind of reason: 999999 life each way makes both life figures land on a bar that cannot visibly move. The Rabbit's Foot is worn last, so every gold and silver card in the deck reads 2 IN 5 rather than 1 IN 5 on its tooltip and pays that often - and if anything shocks the duelist, their own miss chance reads 1/2 rather than 1/4, which is the drawback the relic is honest about. Round one heals nothing either way, since nothing in the game heals above full.

Does the Singular Ring pay on a No Hand, now that the rung is called no-hand rather than high-hand? Wear it and queue the Skewer on its own: one attack card forms no rung of two or more, so the turn is the catalog's No Hand at its 1x, and the ring's add-hand-dmg puts 2 on the duelist's DMG for that one turn - every figure the hit prints is already the raised one. Two cards that agree on nothing are still a No Hand, and the Cut and the Thump are that pair: different concept, different form, different element. Queue the Thump beside the Bash instead and the rung is a Pair, the ring is silent, and the hits say so - which is the comparison to make, since a bonus folded into DMG is only visible against the turn that did not get it. A dummy, so the fight cannot end while the three readings are tried against each other.

The Twinned Ring against the hits that show what it did. Every element in the hand is different and every concept is, so the only rung any selection can form is a form Pair - queue the Smash beside the Bash and both are crush: the ring raises the duelist's DMG by 2 before the hand is counted, the figure flies out of the ring onto the duelist card, and both hits are then worked out at 12 rather than 10. The Skewer on its own is the control: a No Hand, nothing raised, and the same card written at 10. What to watch is that the raise is one climb on the duelist rather than a term of its own - two cards in the hand means the ring is worth twice what it says, which is the whole reason it stopped being a flat addition. A dummy, so both readings can be tried against each other for as long as they are interesting.

The two levels a relic can pay at, in one turn. The Twinned Ring raises the DUELIST - a Pair is worth 2 more DMG, and every hit is worked out at 12 rather than 10 - where Fire scales a CARD, so it is a factor inside one hit and not the other. Queue the Smash beside the Bash: both are crush so the rung is a Pair, the ring's 2 flies onto the duelist card first, and the hits then read the fire card at 12 x 3 x 2 and the ice card at 12 x 2, which is the whole distinction drawn in two lines side by side. Every element in the hand is different, so exactly one card is fire and the contrast between the two brackets is visible. The Skewer on its own is still the control: a No Hand, no raise, no fire, one bare hit. A dummy, so the readings can be tried against each other.

The Jar of Earth on a bench, so the term it adds can be watched moving. It reads the earth cards LEFT IN HAND rather than the ones played - 5 DMG a card - so it is the one relic here that pays for what a turn did not do, and the only way to read its arithmetic is to play a different number of cards and watch the sum. Six of the eight cards in hand are earth and the whole deck is, so the held count is the earth left behind: the fire Slice and the ice Bash pay the jar nothing whether they are played or kept, which is what makes the term readable against a hand that is not all one color. Hold all six earth and the jar is worth 30; play five of them and it is worth 5. That is the tension the fixture is for - playing more raises the hand's own multiplier and shrinks the jar's term at the same time, and the two move against each other inside one sum. The bonus lands in the base rather than on top, so the rung multiplies it like every other term: the same three cards held are worth more behind an Elemental Five of a Kind than behind a Pair. The Brace is in the hand on purpose - a defend card carries an element and brings no damage, so keeping it back pays the jar exactly as keeping an attack does. Against a dummy at 15 AP, so the choice is which cards rather than which are affordable, and the fight does not end while the combinations are being tried.

Ten essences in the consumables pane - five Essence of Strength, five Essence of Weakness - carried into a duel rather than spent at a reward. Select one card in the hand, click an essence, and the card walks its own form's ladder a rung. The question it exists for is the two ends: the ladder is a ring, so demoting the Poke gives an Impale and promoting the Impale gives a Poke, and the same round trip runs on Flinch and Guard down the defend ladder. The eight cards are the two ends of the stab ladder, the two ends of the defend ladder, and four middles, which is what says a rung in the middle still just steps. Nothing goes dim for being pointless - an essence is lit whenever exactly one card is selected - so a wasted pick is the player's to make. Against a dummy at 15 AP, so the hand can be walked up and down for as long as it is interesting.

The Rampant worn alone, with a purse to scale against: +1 duelist DMG for each vitae, so 40 vitae swings the whole hand at DMG plus 40 and every card grows by its own multiplier. The fight is a dummy so the scaling can be watched over as many rounds as it takes, and two Add Vitae runes are in the sack so the purse can be moved mid-fight to see whether the bonus follows it.

Smoldering Jar and Jar of Ice worn together, each +5 duelist DMG for every card of its color kept in hand. The hand is three fire and two ice cards to hold and three earth and lightning attacks to play, so playing the three and keeping the five raises DMG by 25 before a card is scored - one climb on the duelist card, with both jars shaking, and every hit growing by its own card's multiplier. Play a fire card instead and the raise drops by 5. A dummy, so it can be tried as many rounds as it takes.
